newsitem.title: UK: Oil stays near high as U.S. ups Iraq stakes.
newsitem.headline: Oil stays near high as U.S. ups Iraq stakes.

text.p: World oil prices clung to post-Gulf War highs on Friday as nervous oil traders showed little inclination to sell amid widespread anticipation of U.S. military action against Iraq at the weekend.

With U.S. fighter planes heading to the Gulf and Baghdad and Washington still exchanging angry words, traders were on alert for any news of U.S. attacks to punish Iraqi President Saddam Hussein for defying U.S. patrols of no-fly zones.
"I wouldn't be a seller in this market. If there is action over the weekend then prices will rally again," said Peter Bogin at Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA) in Paris.

World benchmark Brent crude oil futures traded as high as $24.24 a barrel, up 37 cents on the day and only 15 cents off Wednesday's peak. This was the highest prompt price on London's International Petroleum Exchange since January 1991 when U.S.-led allies launched their successful Gulf war to liberate Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.

Oil prices rallied nearly $2 a barrel this week as military action over Iraq raised fears of disruption to vital fuel supplies from the Gulf, which contains nearly 70 percent of the world's oil reserves and accounts for about a quarter of output.

"The problem is that Saudi Arabia is about the only oil producer who has spare capacity so any tension in that area is likely to keep prices firm," said Bob Finch, head of trading in London at oil-trading and refining company Vitol SA.
Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil producer and exporter and its 8.0 million barrel per day (bpd) output makes use of about 80 percent of its capacity.
Extension of the conflict to neighbouring producer Kuwait -- which anaylsts consider unlikely given the might of the U.S. military presence in the region -- would drive prices considerably higher.
Baghdad has described Kuwait's decision to allow the United States to station advanced Stealth fighters in the small state occupied by Iraq in 1990 as an act of war.
A government-controlled newspaper on Friday hurled insults at U.S. President Bill Clinton, accusing him of escalating tension for electoral purposes.

But even without a significant escalation of the conflict, traders and analysts do not expect prices to retreat in the short term as western demand gathers pace ahead of winter, industry stocks stay low and non-OPEC supply disappoints.

The indefinite postponement of a U.N. deal that would allow Baghdad's return to the oil market in a limited capacity for the first time since its invasion of Kuwait nearly six years ago would also continue to provide solid support, they said.

The accord, signed on May 20, would have allowed Iraq to sell some $2 billion worth of oil over six months -- equivalent to about 700,000 bpd -- to raise money for food and other much-needed humanitarian supplies.

"Given the approaching U.S. presidential elections, it now seems increasingly likely that Iraqi oil exports will remain shut off until at least early 1997, which in turn adds up to a "loss' of 60-80 million barrels of Iraqi oil," said Kleinwort Benson in a market report.

"Two or three years ago this would have been extra oil but in the autumn of 1996 it is highly desirable and there is no sign yet from Saudi Arabia that it will make up for that 700,000 bpd - it prefers to see these prices continue," said Bogin.

The U.N. Security Council on Thursday renewed its backing for the deal but was too divided to issue a formal statement telling the U.N. Secretary-General to implement the plan as soon as possible, as Italy had proposed.
Analysts said the chances of Iraqi oil sales would become clearer once the smoke of any retaliatory action by the United States has cleared and Iraq's reaction is known.
